messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan still recalls the day his life changed forever. He was 32 years old when he was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of leukemia. The months that followed were a blur of hospital visits, chemotherapy sessions, and endless tests. His body felt like it was under siege, and he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was running out of time. As he began to recover, Rohan started to notice a growing sense of unease within himself. He had always been an optimistic person, but now he found himself consumed by negative thoughts about his own worth. There is something wrong with me as a person, he would often think to himself. This feeling of being defective seeped into every aspect of his life, making him withdrawn and isolated. His fear of being weak and vulnerable also intensified. He became convinced that he was no longer capable of handling physical stress, and situations that put his body under strain made him anxious. Rohan started avoiding activities that he used to enjoy, like hiking or playing sports with friends. He even stopped going to the gym, fearing that any exertion would trigger a relapse. As these avoidance behaviors took hold, Rohan's perception of safety began to erode. Even when his loved ones reassured him that he was safe, he couldn't shake off the feeling that something bad was lurking around the corner. His wife would try to calm him down, saying "you're okay, you're in remission," but Rohan just couldn't trust it. He felt like his body was constantly on alert, tense and ready to react to danger at any moment. This sense of unease only grew stronger when things didn't go according to plan. When a project at work took longer than expected, Rohan would assume that something had gone terribly wrong. His mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios, and he would become convinced that his life was once again under threat. As the months went by, these patterns of thinking only intensified. Rohan started avoiding medical cues altogether – hospitals, ambulances, even physical examinations made him anxious. He stopped going for check-ups, fearing what the doctors might find. His avoidance behaviors became a self-reinforcing cycle: the more he avoided, the more he felt like he was in danger, and the more he felt like he was in danger, the more he avoided. Rohan's emotional numbness also deepened. He felt dead inside, like he was just going through the motions of daily life without any real purpose or passion. His relationships suffered as a result – his wife felt like she was losing him, and his friends didn't know how to reach out. It was only when Rohan's avoidance behaviors started affecting his work that he realized he needed help. As a UX designer, he was used to being creative and problem-solving, but now he found himself struggling to meet deadlines and collaborate with colleagues. His fear of physical stress had become so debilitating that he couldn't even sit in front of a computer for more than an hour without feeling overwhelmed. Rohan finally sought therapy when his wife staged an intervention. She told him that she couldn't watch him slip away anymore, and that she needed her husband back. Rohan was afraid of what the future held, but he knew he had to face his fears head-on. He was tired of living in a state of constant threat, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. With therapy, he hoped to find a way to break free from this cycle of avoidance and fear, and rediscover the person he used to be.
